title: By 28
subtitle: Twenty moments. One person.
intro:
You get twenty chances to arrange the world around Nell Moss. A parent has time, or doesn't. Someone laughs. A door stays open. You choose what happens. Nell keeps her own version.

Some details will get larger. Others will disappear before she knows they were worth keeping. By twenty-eight, she'll have explanations for herself. A few might even be right. You can ask her. You can also look at the record. They won't always agree.

character.name: Nell Moss
character.privateBrief: Nell grows up in an English-speaking household in an unnamed former manufacturing town. Her mother, Jean, works at a laundry. Her father, Martin, repairs council buildings. Their rented flat has a kitchen drawer for instructions, receipts, dead batteries, and things nobody can identify. Money is uneven, affection practical, and neither parent is uniformly wise. Jean talks when tired; Martin can mistake solving a problem for hearing it. Mrs Beck lives downstairs. Kit becomes Nell's school friend at nine and remains an acquaintance through adulthood regardless of the choices. Eli is an adult friend introduced at twenty-two, with no required romantic relationship. Nell notices scraps of everyday language, but whether she shows this interest, protects it, or pursues it is shaped by the life. Adult employment stays unspecified beyond paid work. No path requires marriage, children, a degree, or a particular diagnosis.
character.publicSetup: Nell Moss lives above an empty shop with her parents, Jean and Martin. The shop's sign is still there. Nobody knows why. Jean works at a laundry; Martin repairs buildings for the council. Mrs Beck downstairs lets the postman leave parcels in her hall, then complains about the parcels. Nell is four. She can reach the kitchen counter if she stands on a chair. This is about to become relevant.

tags.definition: A mistake was handled without making Nell herself the problem.
Nell was left to complete a difficult practical task without support.
An act of care came with an explicit financial or social cost.
A question was dismissed or stopped rather than explored.
Attention or affection was explicitly attached to achievement.
Another person joined a practical task without taking it entirely over.
Money or limited access directly constrained an opportunity.
Someone took an unusual interest of Nell seriously.
An interest or project was protected by keeping it private.
Receiving assistance made Nell visible to an audience.
An adult made a definite promise and failed to keep it.
Someone acknowledged an error and made a concrete repair.
A public incident left evidence or an account in other hands.
Nell was made aware of her body through comparison or commentary.
A stated boundary was respected in practice.
A request for freedom or privacy was answered with relational guilt.
Nell retained control of a plan by limiting who knew it.
Work or obligations continued despite explicit physical exhaustion.
Another person publicly supplied words or motives Nell had not supplied.
A later environment made an old social expectation less applicable.

chapters.title: The kitchen drawer
chapters.transitionAfter: The drawer still closes if someone pushes the batteries to the back. Nell is taller now. Adults have started saying she should know better, without mentioning when the knowing was supposed to happen.

chapters.title: Other people present
chapters.transitionAfter: School keeps records of the things it considers important. Nell has received marks for handwriting, attendance, and running. There is no box for what happened after somebody laughed. That goes somewhere else.

chapters.title: Reasonable requests
chapters.transitionAfter: People begin asking Nell what she plans to do with her life. They ask while rinsing mugs, while checking the time. Apparently a life is something she ought to have ready to explain.

scenes.title: The blue saucer
scenes.prompt: Nell has been told to leave the blue saucer alone. It has a little house painted on it, with a door smaller than her fingernail. She wants to see the back. Now it is on the kitchen floor in five pieces, and Martin is in the doorway. The piece with the house has survived. Nell is holding it as though this might count in her favour.

choices.label: Martin puts down his bag, checks her hands, and lets her hold the dustpan while he sweeps.
choices.outcome: Martin sweeps up the saucer with Nell. He puts the surviving house piece on the windowsill. Jean later asks why there's broken crockery beside the basil.

memories.text: She keeps the sound of the bag hitting the floor. In her version, he could have done something else with that hand. The dustpan comes later, after a pause that has grown longer.
The house piece sits in a patch of sun. She remembers being permitted to keep it, although she didn't ask. For a while, the windowsill seems like a reasonable place for damaged things.
Martin's shoes make a scraping noise beside hers. She remembers the saucer having more pieces than it did. The house is still whole. This seems important enough to mention twice.

choices.label: Martin says the saucer mattered to Jean, then sits beside Nell while they gather all the pieces.
choices.outcome: Martin explains whose saucer it was. He helps Nell collect every piece. They leave the pile on a plate for Jean, who sorts it before throwing it away.

memories.text: The saucer belongs to somebody in every version she tells. Her own hands are the difficulty. She has trouble remembering that Martin stayed on the floor until they found the last piece.
Jean has to lose something, and Nell has to stand nearby while she loses it. She remembers the two of them making a small pile together. Nobody leaves her alone with it.
She remembers learning that a thing could matter before she touched it. Martin's knee cracks when he stands up. In later tellings, that crack sometimes belongs to the saucer instead.

choices.label: Martin keeps his work call going and points Nell toward the brush without coming into the kitchen.
choices.outcome: Nell gathers the larger pieces and leaves the dust for Jean. Martin finishes his call. Nobody notices the house fragment Nell puts behind the bread bin.

memories.text: She remembers doing the whole job, even the dust. The brush was nearly as tall as her. Each telling removes a little more of the mess Jean had to finish.
The call lasts through the entire memory. She can't remember the man's name on the other end, but she remembers that he had Martin's attention and she had a brush.
The house goes behind the bread bin. She remembers this as a hiding place she invented. It was also the nearest place she could reach without getting back on the chair.

scenes.title: Special occasion shoes
scenes.prompt: The new shoes are for Jean's cousin's wedding. They make Nell look tidy, which everyone agrees is an improvement. By the time the photographs are finished, the left heel has rubbed through her sock. She keeps lifting that foot while the adults talk. Jean has half a sandwich wrapped in a napkin and a long trip home ahead of her. The bride wants one more photograph.

choices.label: Jean gives Nell a plaster and asks her to finish the photograph before changing into her old shoes.
choices.outcome: The plaster folds inside the heel. Nell stands for the photograph, then changes shoes beside the car. Her smile makes her look older than five.

memories.text: The old shoes are waiting in a bag. This becomes a promise that the unpleasant part has an end. The plaster, which does very little, receives considerable credit in later accounts.
She remembers being told exactly how long she had to manage. One photograph. Later, difficult things often arrive in these little units. The person measuring them usually has comfortable feet.
The photograph is kept on the mantel for years. Looking at it, she sometimes feels the heel again. Nobody else has that problem with the photograph. They say she looks sweet.

choices.label: Jean buys soft shoes nearby, then mentions the extra expense whenever someone compliments Nell's outfit that afternoon.
choices.outcome: Nell gets shoes that don't hurt. Jean tells three relatives what the replacement pair cost. Two praise Jean's resourcefulness. One says children don't understand money.

memories.text: The price outlasts the shoes. It becomes one of the first numbers she knows about herself, and follows her through an otherwise pleasant afternoon. Jean's relatives remember the rabbit, if anything.
She remembers Jean finding a shop when the shoes were wrong. The complaints become the sort of noise adults make while fixing things. In this telling, everybody ends up reasonably satisfied.
The soft shoes are white, with a badly printed rabbit. Nell can walk again. Years later, she remembers the rabbit looking apologetic. It was only missing part of an eye.

choices.label: Jean misses the next photograph to loosen the shoe and sit with Nell on the church steps.
choices.outcome: Jean takes the shoes off and lets Nell eat the sandwich on the steps. The bride sends a photograph later. Jean and Nell are both missing from it.

memories.text: The buckle is a problem Nell expects to solve herself. Jean's hands get there first. Later she tells this as a small surprise, without finding a good way to explain the surprise.

The shoes cost money. Nell remembers that first, and Jean's thumb under the strap second. She sometimes leaves out the photograph they missed, as though being comfortable required no other arrangement.
There is mustard on the napkin and a dent in the step. She remembers the sandwich being hers. It was Jean's lunch, cut in half without an announcement.

scenes.title: Why it follows
scenes.prompt: On the bus, Nell asks why the moon keeps following them. Martin says it doesn't. Nell points out that it is still there. At home she brings him a drawing of the bus, the moon, and several arrows. The arrows are doing a lot of work. Martin has a leaking tap to fix before bed. Nell has drawn herself in every window of the bus.

choices.label: Martin admits he doesn't know and gives Nell paper while he works, without offering to solve it together.
choices.outcome: Nell draws until the paper runs out. Martin finishes the tap. The moon remains unexplained. In the morning, Mrs Beck says perhaps it likes their bus.

memories.text: She remembers being supplied with paper as a form of being left alone. There are worse forms. By morning, her drawings have become an answer she isn't sure anyone needs to see.

Not knowing was something Martin could say out loud. The paper seems like an invitation, though he never looks at the drawings. This version is generous about his intentions, helped by the afternoon Jean stayed on the steps.
Mrs Beck's explanation is the easiest to picture. Nell remembers it for years, sometimes as a joke, sometimes as something a grown woman genuinely believed. Mrs Beck never has to clarify.

choices.label: Martin leaves the tap until tomorrow and helps Nell look for an explanation in an old library book.
choices.outcome: The book's diagram takes both of them a while. They make a second drawing. The tap drips all night, and Jean puts a cloth in the sink.

memories.text: The tap drips through an evening nobody quotes a price for. Martin has given the time to the question anyway. In Nell's version, the book contains a cleaner explanation than either of them actually finds.

Being stuck brings someone closer this time. Martin makes the same wrong guess she does. That guess survives longer than the explanation. Years later she can still explain why the two of them were wrong.
The bus drawing takes up most of the kitchen table. She remembers the moon following for several more journeys, even after the book says otherwise. Knowing hasn't entirely changed the view.

choices.label: Martin gives her a quick answer, says the matter is settled, and returns to fixing the tap.
choices.outcome: Martin says distant things appear to move less. Nell asks what distant means. He repeats the answer more loudly. The tap is fixed before bedtime.

memories.text: The answer has a set length, like the photograph. Her question can continue until it uses up its share of time. Nell starts trying to get the important part into the first sentence.
The tap needs fixing. Sometimes Nell uses this fact to make the evening kinder than it was. The answer still doesn't make sense, but the kitchen becomes quiet afterward, and she likes that part.
The word distant stays with her. It feels like something adults can put between themselves and a question. She can't remember how far away the moon actually is.

scenes.title: The good one
scenes.prompt: Nell has made a box from a cereal packet at school. There is no lid that fits it, but the teacher has written careful work underneath. Jean sees the comment while clearing the table. She has spent the afternoon correcting a trainee at the laundry and is unusually pleased to find evidence of competence at home. Nell waits to see where the box will be put.

choices.label: Jean buys a proper storage box to replace it and praises Nell for giving her the idea.
choices.outcome: Jean moves the cereal box into the kitchen drawer. The new box holds the household receipts. Nell is thanked for solving a problem she hadn't known existed.

memories.text: She remembers the original being put away as soon as the better version arrives. For years she calls this encouragement. She isn't sure why encouragement makes her look inside the drawer afterward.
She remembers an idea turning into a thing the household uses. The purchased box seems like a continuation of hers. This leaves out the afternoon she spent trying to make the corners hold.
The proper box has a lid that clicks. Nell remembers being asked whether she liked it. She wasn't. Jean said she did, and Nell had no obvious reason to interrupt.

choices.label: Jean displays the box and tells visitors Nell is the reliable one, the child who never needs chasing.
choices.outcome: The box goes beside the television. Jean shows the teacher's comment to Mrs Beck. Nell gets asked to bring her next school project home as well.

memories.text: At last she has handed Jean something that brings its own explanation. Careful work. No questions to fit around the tap. The box becomes proof that she can be easy to have in the kitchen.
The box ought to be worth something. Jean's good mood has no price attached, which makes it harder to produce again. Nell remembers making the next box with considerably more attention to the lid.
The lid never fits. In her memory it does, neatly, and the teacher has underlined careful. Years later she finds the box and discovers that neither improvement was made on paper.

choices.label: Jean asks Nell to show her how it was made, including the part where the lid went wrong.
choices.outcome: They make another box after dinner. Jean's is worse. Martin puts screws in both of them, and neither adult mentions the teacher's comment again that week.

memories.text: For once a question isn't being ended quickly. Explaining the lid takes longer than making it. Jean listens with glue on her finger and doesn't pretend to understand before Nell has found the words.

A damaged-looking thing turns out to be useful. Martin's screws don't mind the lid. In later tellings the boxes get bigger, proper containers rather than cereal packets failing to hold a square shape.
Jean's box leans sideways. Nell remembers laughing at it without having to check Jean's face first. The laugh is easier to keep than the instructions, which she eventually forgets.

scenes.title: The envelope
scenes.prompt: The school sends home an envelope for a museum trip. The amount due is printed in a cheerful bubble, beside a cartoon coach. Jean has written electricity on another envelope. Both are on the table. Nell knows which one adults will open first. At school, the teacher has already asked everybody what they want to see. Nell said the room with the old household objects.

choices.label: Jean borrows the fare from Mrs Beck, who asks Nell to tell her everything about the museum afterward.
choices.outcome: Mrs Beck lends the money. Nell goes on the trip and later spends an hour describing old irons. Jean repays Mrs Beck over the next three weeks.

memories.text: The museum must be described properly if it is to remain paid for. Mrs Beck never says this. Nell supplies the rule, then includes every iron she can recall, with an account of their handles.

She remembers money moving between the flats without anyone collapsing. Mrs Beck's questions become a pleasant part of the trip. Jean's repayments disappear from the account entirely, though they were real enough.
The museum has an iron almost too heavy to lift. Nell remembers Mrs Beck wanting to hear about it. Years later she can't remember whether Mrs Beck was interested or simply being owed a conversation.

choices.label: The teacher waives the fee quietly, but asks Nell to help tidy the classroom during the lunch break.
choices.outcome: Nell goes to the museum without paying. At lunch she straightens chairs while the teacher eats. The teacher thanks her and tells her not to mention the arrangement.

memories.text: Tidying becomes the price of admission, a sensible arrangement for somebody capable of careful work. The teacher's instruction to keep quiet gets improved into proof that Nell was trusted with an important matter.
She remembers getting to see the old objects after all. Straightening the chairs occupies very little space in the version she tells. The teacher becomes more generous with every year that passes.
She remembers the room being empty except for the two of them. An arrangement is easier to accept without an audience. Later she dislikes anyone making a fuss about a favour.

choices.label: The fare stays unpaid, and Martin spends the afternoon helping Nell inspect old objects from the kitchen drawer.
choices.outcome: Nell stays at school during the trip. At home, Martin explains a fuse, a door key, and a receipt for something nobody owns anymore. The drawer will not shut afterward.

memories.text: Martin answers every question about the fuse. The missing trip stays missing, but the afternoon supplies a second account of how he can be when there is nowhere else he has to hurry.

She remembers pretending the drawer was better than the museum. It may even have been better in places. The pretending is what she returns to, especially the effort to make Martin's afternoon worthwhile.
The receipt is for a kettle from before she was born. It feels unreasonable that the paper outlasted the kettle. She remembers keeping it for a while, though nobody asked her to.

scenes.title: Milk, milk, milk
scenes.prompt: Nell finds a shopping list in a supermarket trolley. Someone has written milk three times. She takes it home. By Friday she has seven lists, including one that says something nice, underlined. At school, Kit sees them inside her exercise book. Kit sits next to her because their surnames are close enough for the seating plan. This is the first interesting thing the seating plan has produced.

choices.label: Kit shows the lists to the class, where several children offer their own and others call the collection rubbish.
choices.outcome: Nell gets four new lists and a nickname she doesn't like. Kit says the new lists make it worth it. Nell puts the collection away before the next lesson.

memories.text: Defending the collection feels like having entered it for a prize. Four new lists ought to count as success. Nell repeats the calculation until it almost covers what the nickname is doing to the afternoon.

She remembers more of the children bringing paper than the ones laughing. Kit's confidence leaks into the account. The nickname becomes something stupid that happened around a thing she still enjoyed.
The new lists are better than hers. Somebody's mother has written cream for Dad's feet. She remembers enjoying that privately while pretending the whole collection had become embarrassing to her.

choices.label: Kit says the lists are strange, then offers to keep them in a spare folder where nobody else will see.
choices.outcome: Kit gives her a folder with a broken elastic strap. The lists stay out of sight. At lunch they discuss ordinary school things, with the folder between their bags.

memories.text: Strange becomes the verdict; the folder is an appeal. Later Nell tells this as rejection, leaving out the fact that Kit brought the folder from home. It is easier to give the afternoon one intention.
She remembers the folder as a better bread bin: a place for a thing nobody else needs to handle. Kit has helped without asking to see every piece. That distinction stays useful.
The broken elastic leaves a black mark on her thumb. She remembers being relieved the lists had somewhere to go. She can't quite remember whether they were being protected or put away.

choices.label: Kit brings in a list from home and spends lunch guessing who wrote each of Nell's scraps.
choices.outcome: They sort the lists on a lunch table. Kit's father has written bin bags on the back of a photograph. They agree this counts and keep it.

memories.text: Kit asks questions without requiring an account of what the hobby is for. An hour passes without a proper explanation. Nell keeps it as one of the first hours she didn't have to earn.
She remembers showing Kit just three lists, though all seven were on the table. Her memory keeps a reserve. Even the good afternoon needs something that didn't leave her hands.
The photograph shows half a dog. They decide the other half must be with the bin bags. Nell remembers laughing hard enough to get food on one list. The stain remains part of it.

scenes.title: Show your working
scenes.prompt: The maths sheet is nearly finished. Nell has answers for the first nine questions and a blank square for the tenth. The instruction says show your working. She has been showing it for forty minutes. Around her, chairs scrape as children take their sheets up. The teacher asks who still needs help. Nell raises a hand low enough that she could claim she was adjusting her sleeve.

choices.label: The teacher supplies the answer on a separate slip and promises Nell can catch up if she practises at home.
choices.outcome: Nell fills the blank square. At home, Martin checks the answer against the slip but can't explain it. The homework is complete when it goes back.

memories.text: A finished page is a satisfactory result. No blank square, no raised hand. Nell remembers the tick more clearly than the slip. The missing explanation seems less urgent once the sheet has been returned.
She remembers trying to use the slip as an explanation and discovering it contained only a number. This is a disappointing kind of paper. She keeps looking for the part someone must have left out.
The answer is twenty-four. For years she knows that number without knowing the question. It feels like information she should be able to use, provided she finds the right place.

choices.label: The teacher pulls up a chair and works through a different example with Nell before leaving her to finish.
choices.outcome: Nell gets the last answer wrong, but the steps are clearer. The teacher marks the steps and asks her to try again tomorrow. Her sheet is returned with everyone else's.

memories.text: An explanation usually comes with a small job attached. This one doesn't. The teacher just puts the chair back. Nell gives the help a price afterward by becoming especially quiet in the next few lessons.

She remembers the teacher keeping their voices low. An unfinished thing can be opened without being shown to everybody. She starts to distinguish an explanation from an exhibition, though she doesn't call it either.
The teacher draws a badly shaped rectangle. Nell remembers this more fondly than the correct answer, which she never remembers at all. The rectangle makes the sheet seem less official.

choices.label: The teacher uses Nell's unfinished question as a class example, with her name written above it on the board.
choices.outcome: The class solves the question. Nell copies the answer, and three children ask afterward why she found it difficult. One admits he copied all ten.

memories.text: The lists and the blank square become the same public object. Her name sits at the top of both, though only the board actually carries it. The next raised hand takes some preparation.
She remembers the boy who copied admitting it beside her desk. This makes the board smaller in the telling. A correct answer is apparently not a reliable account of how somebody got there.
Her name stays on the board until the next lesson. She remembers other children looking up at it, although most were already packing their bags. The chalk takes longer to erase in memory.

scenes.title: Saturday
scenes.prompt: Martin has promised to take Nell swimming on Saturday. The pool's leaflet is held to the fridge with a magnet advertising a plumber. Nell has folded a towel into her bag. On Saturday morning, Martin gets called to a council building with a burst pipe. He can't go. The towel stays folded. Jean says there's still time to do something with the afternoon, if somebody decides what.

choices.label: Martin names what he promised, apologises, and arranges another adult to take Nell while he pays the entry fee.
choices.outcome: Mrs Beck takes Nell to the pool. Martin leaves money for both fares and entry. Nell swims, and Mrs Beck reads a magazine whose pages become damp.

memories.text: She remembers Martin explaining the arrangement rather than handing over a completed answer. There are still parts she doesn't like. His apology survives because it doesn't require her to call the Saturday perfect.

The fares sit beside the entry fee. Martin has paid for his broken promise, which seems orderly enough. His apology gets shorter each time Nell tells the story, until the payment does most of the work.
Mrs Beck can't swim and has no wish to learn. Nell remembers how long she stays anyway. In some versions Martin is there too, because she remembers telling him about it afterward.

choices.label: Martin promises next Saturday instead, then explains at dinner how many people needed him at the damaged building.
choices.outcome: The towel goes back in the cupboard. Martin describes the flooded offices over dinner. Next Saturday remains unbooked. Nell knows more about the pipe than the pool.

memories.text: She ought to understand because she is reliable. The flooded offices become a test she can't fail without looking childish. The story loses the moment when she almost asks about next Saturday again.

She remembers being interested in the pipe despite herself. This complicates the complaint. The useful part of the evening eventually makes Martin seem less dismissive than his unbooked promise deserved.
In her version, Martin says nobody had a choice. He doesn't quite say it in those words. They are the words she finds afterward, and they explain the evening efficiently.

choices.label: Jean offers the bus fare and a leaflet of nearer activities, leaving Nell to work out an alternative afternoon.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the bus to the library and spends an hour looking at local leaflets. Jean asks where she went. Martin assumes the afternoon has sorted itself out.

memories.text: She remembers finding a leaflet worth showing Kit. A ruined afternoon can still produce something. Martin gradually drops out of the account, although his promise is the reason she was at the library.

The bus fare means she can stop waiting. Independence is a more pleasant word than cancellation. The towel disappears from this version, although its neatly folded shape continues to turn up when she thinks about Saturday.
The library is warm and smells faintly of wet coats. She remembers choosing it. This is true, although her choices began after the one she wanted had been removed.

scenes.title: A noise in the room
scenes.prompt: Nell is reading a passage aloud when her voice catches. A word comes out with a squeak attached. Someone laughs, then apologises too quickly. Nell tries the word again. It is no longer a useful word. It is an object everybody is waiting for her to pick up. The teacher has the book open on her desk. Kit is looking very hard at the window.

choices.label: The teacher makes a joke to ease the room, then has Nell repeat the word until everybody settles.
choices.outcome: Nell gets the word out on the fourth attempt. The teacher congratulates her. At lunch, one child repeats the squeak; another tells him to stop.

memories.text: A whole class seems to join in, though most never do. The old nickname supplies extra voices. Years later Nell has to make a deliberate effort to separate the children in these two rooms.
She remembers the child who says stop. His voice gets louder in the account while the squeak gets smaller. She doesn't remember his name, which makes the rescue seem less like a transaction.
The teacher says there, you can do it. Nell remembers there as a place she has been forced to arrive. The actual word drops out of memory almost at once.

choices.label: The teacher asks whether Nell wants to continue, with the whole class waiting to hear her answer.
choices.outcome: Nell nods and finishes the passage quickly. The teacher thanks her for carrying on. Kit walks beside her to lunch without mentioning the reading.

memories.text: She remembers being given a choice that would become public whichever way she answered. She calls this choosing to finish. Later she wonders what the other choice would have sounded like in that room.
Kit's silence is useful company. There is no request for an account of the noise. The walk to lunch grows longer in Nell's telling, so the good part has more space to occupy.
Her nod becomes a spoken yes in later versions. She sounds braver when she tells it. The teacher remembers the passage as having gone well, which is another available version.

choices.label: The teacher reads the next sentence herself and later checks with Nell privately about trying again another day.
choices.outcome: The lesson carries on. After class, the teacher offers another turn without requiring one. Nell returns the book to the shelf and goes to lunch.

memories.text: Her name never reaches the board this time. The teacher gives the room another sentence to hear. Nell keeps that sentence as kinder than it sounded, perhaps because it doesn't have anything to say about her.

She remembers the quiet conversation afterward more clearly than the squeak. In later versions the teacher intervenes sooner. It is a helpful alteration, and impossible to check against the lesson itself.
The window is stuck open. Kit is looking at a wedge of grey sky. Nell remembers the sky from Kit's side of the room, although she never stood there that afternoon.

scenes.title: It fitted in September
scenes.prompt: Nell's school shirt won't button properly. It fitted in September. Jean says this twice, as though the shirt might reconsider. There is a uniform inspection on Monday and a family visit on Sunday. Nell stands in the kitchen while Jean holds the two sides together. The kettle clicks off. Martin asks whether anyone wants tea and receives no answer from either of them.

choices.label: Jean lets Nell choose a different approved cut, while explaining that the extra cost means postponing another purchase.
choices.outcome: Nell chooses a looser shirt with square cuffs. They delay replacing Jean's slippers. At school, the shirt passes inspection without comment.

memories.text: The choice has a tidy cost, as the museum did. The shirt is hers and the slippers aren't new. Nell becomes good at keeping both facts in view, including on afternoons when nobody asks.
She remembers being offered a shape she could live inside without a discussion of why. The delayed slippers remain part of the story, but they don't get to explain everything about it.
The cuffs are too stiff at first. Nell remembers them as exactly right from the beginning. It is pleasant to have chosen something correctly, and the memory smooths out the first week's rubbing.

choices.label: Jean buys a larger shirt and tells the visiting relatives the old one wore out, without discussing Nell's body.
choices.outcome: The new shirt fits. Jean keeps the old one for cleaning cloths. At the family visit, nobody is offered an explanation beyond ordinary wear.

memories.text: Another room ought to be hearing about her soon. Instead Jean gives the relatives a worn shirt. Nell keeps the afternoon as the first time an object was allowed to take the blame for her.
She remembers checking the price tag before trying it on. Jean says nothing about the expense. The silence is easy to forget later because nothing embarrassing happens inside it.
The old shirt becomes a cloth for the windows. Nell remembers using it without recognising it at first. Its second job is easier for everybody, though nobody calls that a success.

choices.label: Jean buys the new shirt but makes Nell's growth a cheerful topic during the family visit.
choices.outcome: Three relatives comment on how Nell is changing. One compares her with Jean at thirteen. The new shirt is comfortable; Nell keeps her cardigan on throughout the visit.

memories.text: The shirt feels like the wedding shoes: a comfortable replacement arriving after everyone has established a version of her. She can't remember who made each remark. In the account, the relatives speak with one voice.
She remembers one relative asking about school afterward. It gives the visit another topic, which she eventually promotes to the main one. The cardigan remains on in every version.
Jean calls the conversation affectionate. Nell remembers the word because it makes objecting sound unreasonable. The shirt has room for her. The afternoon does not seem to have the same provision.

scenes.title: Somebody should write it down
scenes.prompt: Kit has joined a group that meets on Thursdays to watch films at somebody's house. Nell is invited this week. In the group chat, people argue about which film they watched last time. One title appears three times with different spellings. Someone says they need a person who keeps track. Kit has mentioned that Nell is good with paper. A typing bubble sits beneath the suggestion.

choices.label: The host invites Nell but jokes in the chat that nobody should say anything they wouldn't want filed away.
choices.outcome: Nell goes. Two people make exaggerated formal statements when she arrives. The joke wears out before the film starts, and nobody asks about her papers again.

memories.text: The old nickname comes back without being spoken. Nell laughs at the formal statements and later remembers her laugh as agreement. The bag stays zipped through the film, as though it has something to contribute.

The joke ends quickly. She remembers this ending more than its beginning: people are capable of finding another topic without a formal intervention. It is a small fact she sometimes needs to retrieve.
One boy says, for the record, I would like some crisps. Nell remembers him as the whole group for a while. Eventually he shrinks back to one boy eating crisps.

choices.label: The host says Nell can come without taking notes, and sends her the address separately from the argument.
choices.outcome: Nell goes on Thursday. They watch half a film and spend the rest of the evening talking over it. Nobody takes an accurate record of anything.

memories.text: The address stays. An invitation has arrived before she has done anything useful. Years later she sometimes supplies a small task she must have performed, as though the evening needs to balance before she can keep it.
A room where nobody discusses her arrival becomes unusually easy to keep. The people are kinder in her memory than their argument about the film deserves. She gives them that improvement willingly.
She can't remember the film. One person eats a bowl of dry cereal with a serving spoon. This survives intact, taking up more space than most of the conversation.

choices.label: The group asks Nell to maintain its list and includes her in every plan once she agrees.
choices.outcome: Nell is added to the chat. She creates a list with dates and titles. For three weeks, every Thursday plan arrives addressed to her.

memories.text: Dates and titles are easier than an unfinished maths question. A completed page makes people pleased to see her. She keeps the feeling of being wanted and files the practical explanation underneath it.
Kit still sends messages unrelated to the list. Nell keeps these in the account when she starts worrying what the group actually wants. The list is useful, but it doesn't explain every Thursday.
There is a column marked comments which nobody fills in. Nell remembers it as a generous amount of space. Later she laughs at how little the group wanted to preserve of itself.

scenes.title: Nothing to hide
scenes.prompt: Jean has found a folded page while putting clean clothes in Nell's room. It is a letter Nell hasn't sent, with somebody's name crossed out. Jean leaves it on the bed. At dinner she asks who it was for. Nell says she'd rather keep it private. Martin starts buttering bread with attention that would be excessive even if the bread were difficult. Jean waits for a better answer.

choices.label: Jean agrees not to read letters again, then asks Nell to reassure her that they still tell each other everything.
choices.outcome: The letter stays private. Jean asks twice during the week whether Nell has anything to tell her. Nell begins leaving harmless details available at dinner.

memories.text: She supplies a good account of the day, leaving nothing in it that could worry Jean. It takes work. In memory, this starts to count as closeness, because both of them are satisfied afterward.
The letter gets the same treatment as the lists: protected while it stays elsewhere. Relief is the easiest part to remember. Later Nell struggles to explain what else was mixed into it at dinner.
Nobody reads the page again. Nell keeps that fact beside Jean's questions without knowing how to total them. The crossed-out name eventually becomes less interesting than the room around it.

choices.label: Martin installs a lock at Nell's request, while Jean says dinner will be awkward if everyone starts keeping secrets.
choices.outcome: The lock works. Jean does not enter the room without knocking. For several dinners, the ordinary question about school is asked in a careful new tone.

memories.text: Privacy has a shape she can carry now. Martin shows her how the lock works. Jean's remark gets filed under the cost of doing a difficult job yourself, beside a few much older objects.
Martin installs what was requested instead of negotiating a smaller version. Nell remembers the screws going in. The difficult dinners become temporary weather around a thing that continues to work.
The key catches in a hole in her pocket. She remembers it as heavy. It weighs very little, and the pocket is old. These are details she doesn't include when telling the story.

choices.label: Jean says she shouldn't have read it and asks Nell where clean clothes should be left from now on.
choices.outcome: The laundry goes outside Nell's door. Jean occasionally forgets, then takes it back out when reminded. The letter remains on Nell's desk, unsent.

memories.text: Jean does the new thing more than once. Words have been allowed to replace arrangements before, so Nell keeps track of the repetition. The clothes outside the door become better evidence than the apology.

The shirt and the letter belong together in her account: two things Jean could have explained to somebody else and didn't. Nell remembers Jean understanding immediately. The dinner took longer than that.
Jean keeps putting socks on the top of the pile, where they fall off. Nell complains about this. Years later the complaint feels like evidence that the larger request has become ordinary.

scenes.title: Thank you for entering
scenes.prompt: Nell's school project is an interview with a retired caretaker about the houses demolished behind the station. She has transcribed the recording, including the part where he asks if anyone wants a biscuit. It has taken weeks. The project goes to a district competition. The results arrive in a letter that begins thank you for entering. Nell understands the rest before unfolding it all the way.

choices.label: The teacher reads the judges' specific comments with Nell and arranges for the caretaker to receive a finished copy.
choices.outcome: The judges found the project difficult to navigate. Nell labels the sections and sends the caretaker a copy. He phones the school to say his daughter has read it.

memories.text: The comments are awkward but usable, another badly drawn rectangle. She remembers finding something to do after losing. The caretaker's phone call grows more enthusiastic than the teacher's actual report of it.

She remembers the revised copy as a second result, one she can improve by staying up later. The caretaker's daughter becomes another judge. A kindly ending acquires a marking scheme she supplies herself.
He says his daughter read it, nothing more. Nell remembers this plain sentence for years. Someone who wasn't required to has spent time with the thing she made. She has no certificate for it.

choices.label: The teacher says the judging was unfair and encourages Nell to enter a bigger competition with the same project.
choices.outcome: Nell sends the project elsewhere. It is not selected there either. The teacher says the right audience hasn't found it yet. The original comments stay in an envelope.

memories.text: Two rejections become evidence of other people's poor judgement. She remembers the teacher's certainty as confidence in her. It is useful until she needs to decide whether anything in the project should change.

She eventually opens the comments again. In her memory the teacher encouraged this too, though he mostly spoke about larger audiences. The altered account gives her permission to learn something from the letter.
The second envelope looks almost identical to the first. She remembers them as a pair. Thank you for entering begins to sound like a sentence people use when they are done with you.

choices.label: Jean suggests putting the project away for a month and leaves room for it on a shelf without asking what comes next.
choices.outcome: The recording and transcript sit on the shelf. Nell doesn't revise them that month. Other schoolwork continues, and the project remains available without a deadline attached.

memories.text: A thing she made can apparently stop doing a job for a while. She remembers being suspicious of the shelf. Nothing follows the offer, and eventually the absence of a follow-up becomes part of it.
She remembers the shelf as another way to carry on alone, but this time someone has cleared the space deliberately. The distinction isn't visible from across the room. She keeps it anyway.

The envelope slides behind the transcript. When she finds it again, the disappointment is smaller than she expects. She remembers that surprise, though she later makes it sound more deliberate than it was.

scenes.title: A sensible use of paper
scenes.prompt: Nell has an idea for a booklet of ordinary written things: notices, lists, labels, the slips left inside returned books. She has made four pages using new scraps collected that week. Jean finds them beside the printer. The local library has invited proposals for a small display. The form asks who the work is for. Nell has left that field blank. Jean is looking at it.

choices.label: Jean leaves the pages alone after Nell asks, and the library supplies a plain envelope for a private submission.
choices.outcome: Nell submits the pages without a family discussion. Jean knows she has sent something but not what. The acknowledgment arrives in the same plain envelope a week later.

memories.text: She remembers asking once and being allowed to leave it there. The envelope's plainness becomes a kindness. Later she adds a secrecy to the submission that neither Jean nor the library actually required.
The envelope is a better version of Kit's folder, with a whole new room waiting at the other end. She remembers being alone when she posts it. There were other people in the queue.
Nobody asks if the proposal went well. Some days this is exactly what Nell wanted. On other days she carries the acknowledgment into the kitchen and leaves it near the kettle.

choices.label: Jean asks what interests Nell about the pages, then offers to read the proposal without suggesting an audience.
choices.outcome: Jean reads the form and corrects a spelling mistake. Nell submits it with a short explanation of the scraps. The library acknowledges receipt but makes no immediate decision.

memories.text: Milk written three times finally has somewhere to be explained without a nickname attached. She remembers Jean asking good questions. Some were ordinary questions, improved afterward by the fact that Jean stayed to hear the answers.

Jean doesn't promise the right audience will arrive. Nell remembers this as less encouraging at first. Later the small spelling correction feels more useful than a forecast neither of them could check.
The form has a smudge where Jean's hand rests on the paper. Nell remembers waiting for a verdict that never comes. Jean asks whether the printer needs ink. The proposal goes in anyway.

choices.label: Jean tells relatives about Nell's promising design project and asks them to suggest people who could make it useful.
choices.outcome: An uncle recommends leaflets for businesses. Nell gets an offer to design a takeaway menu. Her library proposal goes in without mentioning the offer.

memories.text: The relatives get another subject with her name attached. She remembers smiling while the project changes hands without moving from the table. The menu is useful evidence that they were trying to help.
She remembers the menu as a possible way to pay for paper. A practical offer is easier to defend than the blank field on the form. She starts explaining the work in terms of supplies.
Someone calls the booklet a portfolio. Nell remembers trying the word in her mouth. It makes the scraps sound ready for something, which is pleasant until people begin asking what that something is.

scenes.title: The spare bed
scenes.prompt: A six-month training place is available in the next town. It won't settle Nell's future, but it would give her a way to try something beyond school. She has been offered a cheap room in a shared house. Jean asks whether there is a washing machine. Martin asks about locks. The room's photograph contains a bed, a desk, and an unplugged lamp. Nell keeps enlarging the lamp.

choices.label: Jean offers the deposit only if Nell promises weekly visits and a full account of who lives in the house.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the room and visits weekly. Jean learns the housemates' names. A missed visit prompts a long call about whether the arrangement is still working.

memories.text: She remembers the deposit as another trip that needs reporting afterward. The housemates become like museum objects, described for someone at home. She keeps their more awkward habits out of the account.
The housemates include her in dinner without asking for a report. She remembers these evenings as the part of the room she paid for herself. This is financially inaccurate and emotionally convenient.
The weekly bag gets packed with laundry and suitable stories. Nell remembers the arrangement as practical. It is practical, among other things, and the other things are harder to fold.

choices.label: The deposit cannot be found, but the training provider offers Nell a travel pass so she can commute from home.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the training place and travels each day. She learns the bus timetable by heart. Her room at home stays hers, and evenings are shorter.

memories.text: She remembers the bus as another version of the drawer: what can be done with what is available. The missing room sometimes feels irrelevant. At other times she can describe its photograph exactly.
The lock is still on her bedroom door. She remembers being glad of it after the last bus. There is no new address, but there is a place she can shut off from the account.
She knows which seat gets the heater and which window leaks. In her version the journey becomes time she enjoyed having to herself. This leaves out several mornings she slept through her stop.

choices.label: Jean and Martin help with the deposit and say Nell can return if the place turns out badly.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the room. The lamp works once plugged in. She returns home for occasional meals without needing to describe the training as either a success or a mistake.

memories.text: She remembers waiting for the return offer to acquire a condition. It doesn't. Jean still asks questions, but Nell can come home before answering them properly. This takes several visits to believe.
She tells people she arranged the move herself. The claim leaves out the deposit, which Jean and Martin supplied without asking for the pages. Independence looks cleaner after this small omission.
The lamp has an ugly shade. Nell remembers loving it, though she mostly loves having somewhere to put it. Returning home becomes something she can do without undoing the room.

scenes.title: Available hours
scenes.prompt: Nell has been paid late. The amount is correct, which the payroll email treats as the important part. She has picked up extra hours and fallen asleep sitting on the edge of her bed with one shoe off. Tomorrow's shift begins early. Her supervisor texts to ask whether she can stay longer. Jean has offered dinner. Kit has asked why she keeps answering messages with a full stop.

choices.label: Kit covers dinner and helps find somebody to take the extra hours, though Nell will lose the additional pay.
choices.outcome: A colleague takes the hours. Nell eats with Kit and sleeps that evening. Her immediate bills remain tight, and the next payday is still several days away.

memories.text: She waits for dinner to turn into a discussion of what she ought to do. Kit complains about a broken freezer instead. A meal can apparently end without producing a revised plan for her.
She remembers the hours she didn't work while Kit tells the freezer story. Later she says she slept brilliantly. She did sleep, but the account leaves out how often she checked the banking app first.
Kit serves peas in a mug because the plates are dirty. Nell remembers the mug on the table. There is no ceremony about being looked after, which makes it easier to finish the meal.

choices.label: The supervisor shortens the shift on health grounds and announces the change to the team before Nell can discuss it.
choices.outcome: Nell works fewer hours and gets less pay. Two colleagues ask whether she is all right. The supervisor tells her she can request more hours once she feels better.

memories.text: Her name reaches the room before she does. She remembers the announcement as louder than it was. The reduced hours help, which makes the old irritation harder to present without sounding ungrateful.

She eventually asks to be consulted before the next announcement. In her account she asks immediately. The missing interval contains one awkward shift, two explanations, and a message she writes several times.
One colleague asks quietly and one asks across the room. Nell remembers them as a single inquiry until she has a reason to separate them. The supervisor has already recorded the matter as resolved.

choices.label: The supervisor offers extra pay and a taxi home if Nell covers the longer shift, with no promise of future hours.
choices.outcome: Nell works the shift and takes the taxi. The fare is covered. She has enough money for the immediate bills and eats toast standing by the bed.

memories.text: The figures add up. She remembers the shift as a reasonable exchange and the taxi as a sign she was considered. The toast occupies very little space in this account. She was too tired to taste it.
There was another way to stop for a while, and she knows it. The knowledge doesn't pay the bills. In memory, the fare becomes less generous each time the extra hours are mentioned.
The driver asks whether she's had a long day. Nell says yes. He doesn't need the details, and this is a relief she remembers more vividly than the extra pay.

scenes.title: You can leave that there
scenes.prompt: Eli has come over to return a borrowed adapter. Nell has known them for a few months. While looking for somewhere to plug it in, she moves a notebook off the table. It falls open to a page of unfinished sentences. Some are descriptions. Some are things she meant to say to people. Eli sees enough to ask about it. The adapter is still in its little plastic bag.

choices.label: Eli offers an exact reading of the page, warmly explaining what they think Nell has been afraid to admit.
choices.outcome: Eli's account gets some details right and others wrong. Nell corrects one point. Eli says it makes sense that she'd resist being understood so quickly.

memories.text: Another person improves her explanation before hearing it. Nell remembers the accurate parts as bait, though Eli may have meant every word kindly. The correction she makes gets shorter in each telling.

She remembers waiting for Eli to check the reading with her. Having seen people revise themselves, she gives the evening extra chances in memory. The actual reply to her correction stays inconveniently clear.
Eli says understood as though it is a thing already completed. The notebook is still open. Nell remembers wishing she had written an instruction on the first page, something very plain.

choices.label: Eli offers to read a page if Nell wants, then admits they've been pretending to understand something at work.
choices.outcome: Nell shows one page. Eli describes a mistake they've been hiding. The conversation runs late; the adapter isn't tested, and neither story gets a solution.

memories.text: Nobody offers to turn the page into a portfolio. Eli has an embarrassing story of their own, with no useful ending. Nell remembers the evening as more candid than it probably was. One page still stayed closed.

The conversation feels like the mug of peas: something offered without a correct response attached. She remembers Eli's mistake word for word. Her own unfinished sentences get vaguer, perhaps because she no longer needs to defend them.

Eli's work story includes a meeting where they say certainly four times. Nell laughs at the fifth certainly, which Eli adds on purpose. In memory there is no clear point at which they stop being careful.

choices.label: Eli says the notebook can stay private and keeps the evening to practical matters, without asking again.
choices.outcome: Nell closes the notebook. They test the adapter, find it works, and make tea. Eli leaves without knowing what the unfinished sentences were for.

memories.text: She waits for a question disguised as reassurance. None arrives. The adapter works and the evening remains pleasant. She remembers wanting to reopen the book after it would have seemed odd to do so.
Kit's folder comes back as a closed notebook on a clear table. She remembers Eli as easy company. Years later, easy still means several things, including never having to explain this page.
Tea gets spilled on the plastic bag. Both of them watch a drop run along the sealed edge. The evening is remembered as quiet and good. Something else about it is difficult to specify.

scenes.title: The improved version
scenes.prompt: At a small gathering, Kit tells a story about Nell asking for a favour. The account is funny and mostly recognisable, except for the sentence Nell is supposed to have said. She didn't say it. Everybody laughs at that sentence. Afterward she tells Kit the quote was invented. Kit says it was a better way of putting the same thing. The others are still nearby, collecting their coats.

choices.label: Kit corrects the invented quote in front of the others and later asks Nell how the story should be told.
choices.outcome: The correction is awkward and short. One person admits remembering the invented line already. Kit stops using it and checks before retelling the incident.

memories.text: An improved version can apparently be withdrawn. The words don't disappear from everybody's head, but Kit stops defending them. Nell remembers this distinction with unusual accuracy because she has needed it before.
The correction supplies a second public scene, which she hadn't asked for. In memory it happens quietly, almost privately. The edited account lets her accept a repair that felt exposing at the time.
One person says they preferred the other line. Kit says that's the problem. Nell remembers this exchange better than the original favour. The story becomes something that happened to a story.

choices.label: Kit agrees to stop telling the story but refuses a public correction, saying the group has already moved on.
choices.outcome: The story isn't told again by Kit. Someone else quotes the line once in a message. Nell explains that it wasn't hers, and the exchange ends without an argument.

memories.text: The agreement is kept. The explanation accompanying it stays unpleasant. Nell remembers trying to decide whether the result excuses the conversation, as though there were a rule printed somewhere that would settle this.

She remembers correcting the message plainly and receiving a plain acknowledgment. This small exchange eventually competes with Kit's refusal. The whole group becomes less certain of the false version in her account.
The line is good. Nell admits this privately and dislikes that it matters. She remembers Kit's silence afterward as an apology on some days and a convenience on others.

choices.label: Kit apologises privately, explains why the joke mattered to them, and asks Nell not to make the next gathering tense.
choices.outcome: Nell receives the apology. At the next gathering Kit tells different stories. The invented quote is left uncorrected, and neither of them brings it up there.

memories.text: She remembers being given another small job in exchange for inclusion: keep the room easy. Kit's apology is real, but it arrives with work inside it. She starts checking stories before laughing.

The apology sounds like one she once trusted. She remembers wanting it to do the same work. Kit's changed stories help, though the original sentence continues to belong to her in other people's accounts.
At the next gathering she laughs too promptly. This becomes the embarrassing part she remembers. Kit's invented words recede behind something she really did, which is easier to blame herself for.

scenes.title: Nobody checks the cupboard
scenes.prompt: Nell takes a temporary place in a shared workroom. She wants a table away from whatever else the week is asking of her. On the first evening, someone leaves a half-finished piece out and goes home. Another person uses the kitchen without announcing it. A cupboard contains plates that don't match. Nell asks who keeps track of them. The organiser says the cupboard isn't that kind of problem.

choices.label: The organiser offers Nell a paid role keeping the workroom's records, with free table space and less time for her own pages.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the role for the temporary stay. The accounts become clearer. She has free space but often uses her evenings to check receipts instead of work on her pages.

memories.text: There is a new room and a familiar route into it. She remembers being necessary as belonging. This account is partly true, and easier to maintain than a separate tally of the pages she doesn't finish.
The terms are explained to her before anybody announces the arrangement. Nell remembers liking that she can answer. The work still takes more of the evening than the explanation led her to expect.

The plates remain uncounted while every receipt gets a number. She remembers noticing this inconsistency and leaving it alone. The room is allowed to have different rules for different kinds of evidence.

choices.label: The organiser invites Nell to leave unfinished work out, with a clear warning that other people may see it.
choices.outcome: Nell leaves a page on the table. Someone adds a pencil question on a separate slip. Nobody asks for a finished version before she has one.

memories.text: The page spends a whole night outside its envelope. Nell remembers checking it for interference in the morning. The separate slip gradually becomes a friendlier object because it can be picked up without altering the page.
The question is actually a question. Nobody has answered it on her behalf. She remembers the handwriting as careful, although it is hurried and ugly. This is an improvement she likes making.
The page has curled at one corner. She remembers this as the room doing something to it. The change is minor, and not a criticism, which takes a while to become obvious.

choices.label: The organiser gives Nell a cupboard key and leaves her to use the table without joining the communal evenings.
choices.outcome: Nell keeps her materials locked away and works alone some nights. She can attend the group evenings later if she asks. Nobody checks whether she is enjoying herself.

memories.text: A second key arrives without a difficult dinner attached. Nell remembers how light it feels, though it weighs more than the bedroom key. There is nobody here she has to reassure about using it.

She knows an invitation can exist without a job attached. This one can apparently exist without an immediate answer either. The room feels more available in memory than the evenings she actually spends there.
Nobody asks what is in the cupboard. Nell remembers being pleased about this, and sometimes wishes somebody had asked. Both accounts have the same key lying beside them.

scenes.title: Under your own name
scenes.prompt: A small local publication wants a piece from Nell. They have seen a few pages about ordinary written things and think she could make something longer. The editor sends three possible arrangements. Each includes her name in print. None offers enough money to transform her life. The email is cheerful about this. Nell reads it once on her phone and again at a proper screen, as though the screen might improve the terms.

choices.label: The editor offers a slower schedule and Nell's approval of the heading, but a smaller payment and less prominent placement.
choices.outcome: Nell accepts the slower schedule. She approves a plain heading and sees the piece printed near the back. Some readers never reach it; several do.

memories.text: The smaller audience would once have sounded like the wrong audience. She remembers rereading that assumption before choosing the arrangement. The printed pages are real without requiring the rest of the publication to make room around them.

The terms are limited, and she has practice finding something inside limited terms. In memory the smaller payment becomes unimportant. Her bank account continues to disagree on several ordinary afternoons.

The heading doesn't pretend the pages will change anybody's life. Nell remembers enjoying this. Later she sometimes wonders whether she should have wanted more. The piece stays printed while she wonders.

choices.label: The editor offers a public workshop instead of a finished piece, where Nell can show the pages and hear readers directly.
choices.outcome: Nell takes the workshop. Seven people come. One talks mostly about himself; another stays afterward to discuss a sentence. There is no finished publication at the end.

memories.text: There is another room waiting for her to speak, but this time she knows what the invitation contains. She remembers the seven people as fewer. The change makes the evening easier to tell honestly.

The workshop produces no receipts worth entering and no finished object to file. Nell remembers being bothered by this. Then she remembers the sentence discussed afterward, which has occupied someone else's evening without becoming a result.
The man who talks about himself leaves early. She remembers the woman who stays. For once the account gives somebody time in proportion to what they did with it, rather than how loudly they arrived.

choices.label: The editor offers a paid deadline and a prominent slot, with no opportunity for Nell to approve the final heading.
choices.outcome: Nell accepts and delivers the piece. It is published with a heading she finds overstated. The payment arrives on time, and people she knows ask about it.

memories.text: The heading sounds like an improved version again. Nell asks for a change, knowing such things can be corrected. The editor declines. In memory the asking becomes as important as the refusal.
She has been given a useful name for the work at last. It isn't the name she would have chosen. The payment makes this easier to discuss and harder to decide about.
Her name is spelled correctly. She remembers checking that before reading the heading. It is an embarrassingly small reassurance to keep from the occasion, but she keeps it without improving it.

ending.arrival:
Nell is twenty-eight. There are things she can explain about herself and things she has learned to describe convincingly. She has had some practice.

You can ask her a few questions now. She won't give you a score or a list of causes. She'll answer as the person who was there, which is a different kind of record.

summaries.text: Nell likes an offer better once the details are written down. She checks what has been included and what everybody assumes. People sometimes call this pessimism. She considers it a way to keep the conversation from changing after she has agreed to something.

Nell takes people one arrangement at a time. A kind conversation doesn't settle the next one; a bad afternoon doesn't necessarily settle the person. This makes her slower to describe anyone as dependable, and less surprised when somebody she dislikes does something decent.

Nell usually expects a reply to a request. She can picture somebody making room before she knows exactly how they will manage it. A refusal still hurts. It just doesn't always become an account of what asking was worth in the first place.

The unfinished part is increasingly allowed to exist outside Nell's hands. She can show a page without introducing it as terrible, or admit she hasn't decided. Sometimes the response is disappointing. She no longer has to prevent every such response before anything gets shown.

Nell reads the room before deciding how much of herself belongs in it. She can be quite candid once she knows where a remark will go. Occasionally she waits so long for this information that the moment she wanted to speak in has passed.

Nell often prepares a version she can bear to have repeated. The wanting, the uncertainty, the embarrassing amount of effort stay somewhere behind it. People call her composed. They don't see how many small checks went into letting the composed person arrive.

Nell keeps a close eye on obligations as they begin. A small favour can become a continuing arrangement before anybody names it. She prefers to know what is being asked. There are people who find this cold, and people who find the clear answer useful.

Nell makes room carefully. She can sit with somebody's unfinished account, but doesn't always want to become responsible for completing it. Her care often looks practical: a question answered, a plate set aside. She is still deciding when practical is enough.

Nell notices what would make the next hour easier for someone. She can give it without announcing what sort of person that makes her. Receiving the same attention is less straightforward. There are occasions when she starts doing the washing-up before the kindness has finished.

Nell is less willing to give a whole evening to proving she can do something. A finished object is satisfying, but so is time that nobody has marked. She sometimes worries this is an elaborate excuse. The worry no longer gets to schedule every afternoon.

Nell wants the work to hold up when she looks at it again. She can enjoy doing something well without needing it to explain her life. Some days this feels like a sensible standard. On others she suspects she has placed it conveniently within reach.

Nell wants a result that survives somebody saying well done. She likes evidence, something difficult made properly, an answer she couldn't have supplied last year. Satisfaction tends to be brief. Soon she notices another part that could be done better, and the evening changes shape.

Nell likes to know what an invitation contains before accepting it. Familiar arrangements spare her a particular kind of tiredness. She still notices odd details, but she doesn't have to follow all of them home. Some scraps can remain somebody else's business.

Nell will follow a question if she has somewhere to put down the rest of the day first. She wants a little time, a door she can leave through. With those in place, an unfamiliar thing can become more interesting than its possible inconvenience.

Nell is susceptible to a detail that doesn't fit. A repeated word, a rule nobody explains, a cupboard managed differently from the receipts. She can lose an evening finding out why. Sometimes there is a good answer. Sometimes the evening is what she gets.

tensions.text: She expects people to help and still wants the request worded perfectly. These expectations can occupy the same afternoon. Someone says yes before she has finished preparing, and Nell is left with a reply and several unused ways of making herself easier to accept.

Nell can be generous with people whose promises she won't use to plan a day. She knows what would help them and is less certain they would notice the equivalent in her. Being needed can feel safer than asking for an exchange.

She wants to be good at something without giving uncertainty too much access to the process. A task with a clear standard is attractive. A question that might change the task is less welcome, especially after she has already put in the hours.

There are things she once kept from people that she could show them now. The change doesn't automatically open the old drawer. Nell sometimes discovers she is still protecting an earlier version of a plan nobody presently knows enough to interfere with.

She has seen somebody put a mistake right. She can describe what they did quite accurately. Yet a new apology still arrives without credit from the old one. The repair is kept as an individual occurrence rather than evidence she feels safe using again.

She wants to look inside and doesn't want to be seen looking. This produces elaborate little arrangements: a question asked casually, a page shown by accident. The interest is real. So is the effort to make it appear to have wandered into the room without her.

She no longer wants every pleasant evening to depend on a good result. Part of her still waits to be asked what she has done. On days when nobody asks, relief can come mixed with a small, unreasonable feeling of having been overlooked.

Some rooms have stopped requiring the precautions Nell brings into them. She continues to bring them. A plain invitation gets checked for the task underneath; an empty silence gets filled with an explanation. The room may be easy before she finds a way to be easy in it.

She can remember someone joining a difficult job without taking it over. The memory doesn't mean she wants every problem made communal. Nell prefers small, named arrangements now. She can miss the company in an old scene while declining the same offer this week.

A result can still seem like a way to pay for her place in the room. Nell knows the price of several things that were once supposed to be ordinary. Sometimes she keeps working after the immediate bill is covered, without noticing that the account has changed.

questions.label: What happens when you need help?

low.text: First I try to work out what I'm asking for. Otherwise someone offers the wrong thing and I'm supposed to be pleased. I like a request with edges: this much time, this particular job. I don't think people are incapable of helping. I think it's sensible to make the arrangement difficult to misunderstand.

middle.text: Depends who's there, and what kind of help. I try to ask early enough that it isn't an emergency I've quietly manufactured by refusing to mention it. Then I watch what happens. A yes is useful, but so is somebody telling me plainly what they can actually do. I can plan around that.

high.text: Usually I ask. I might need a minute to work out how, but I assume there's a conversation available. Even if they can't do the thing, they might know a smaller thing that would help. I don't need every request to end well. I do like knowing I can make another one.

questions.label: What makes you hesitate around someone new?

low.text: Mostly whether we'll have anything to talk about after the obvious questions. I don't mind admitting a strange interest if they're going to have one too. The difficult moment is when they start being impressed instead of curious. Then you're stuck maintaining the impressive version, which is a tedious way to spend an evening.

middle.text: I listen to how they talk about somebody who isn't there. If every absent person is ridiculous, I assume I'll eventually be given a turn. I don't need them to be solemn about everyone. I just want to know whether an awkward sentence is going to be kept and passed around later.

high.text: How quickly they decide what I am. Especially if it's flattering. You can get trapped inside a compliment because objecting makes you seem ungrateful. I wait until they've changed their mind about something small. That tells me more than being told I'm interesting by somebody who has heard me speak for six minutes.

questions.label: What does caring for somebody cost you?

low.text: Time, usually. Also the part where a favour stops being a favour and becomes a standing service nobody discussed. I'd rather offer something specific and do it properly. People sometimes think that's ungenerous. But if I say I can do Friday, I mean Friday. I won't quietly start resenting them on Thursday.

middle.text: Attention. If I'm properly listening, the rest of the evening becomes less available. I'm willing to do that, just not for every problem in every room. I used to think the only choices were fixing it or leaving. Sitting there without inventing a solution turns out to be an actual thing you can do.

high.text: Sometimes I give away time I had already spent in my head. A whole quiet evening, gone before anyone knows it was planned. I'm not always sorry. I like making a difficult hour less difficult. I do get awkward if someone notices too much. Then it becomes a performance and I want to put the kettle on.

low.text: That I'd managed the particular thing, I suppose. I'd like it to stop there. Once it becomes proof of what sort of person I am, the next ordinary day starts looking inadequate. I'd rather have a result I can enjoy and then put down. There are other things I want an afternoon to contain.

middle.text: That I hadn't imagined the whole possibility. It's satisfying when something survives the move from an idea to a finished object. I don't need it to prove I was always secretly exceptional. That would be quite a burden to carry into the next attempt, especially while finding somewhere to put the first one.

high.text: That I can do it properly. I know properly sounds like a convenient word because I can keep moving it. Still, there must be a version I could look at without immediately making excuses. I'd like to reach that once. The annoying part is that I have reached it with smaller things and somehow failed to keep the evidence.

questions.label: What could make you change your mind?

low.text: A reason I can use, rather than just a new possibility. There are plenty of possibilities. Following each one is how you end up tired with six tabs open and nothing you needed to do finished. Show me what doesn't work in the present arrangement. I can be interested after that. I don't need to be surprised as a hobby.

middle.text: A detail I can't explain with the version I've got. I'll leave it alone if I'm tired, but it tends to come back. I like having enough time to look at it without somebody requiring a conclusion immediately. Otherwise I might defend the old answer just because I've already found words for it.

high.text: Quite a small thing. A date that doesn't fit, someone using a word strangely, a rule that turns out not to be a rule. Then I want to find the rest. It's inconvenient if I've been very definite about the old explanation. I can usually admit I was wrong before I can stop sounding irritated about it.

questions.label: What happens when somebody lets you down?

low.text: I change the plan so I don't need that particular promise again. Then I listen to the explanation. I know that's the wrong order for some people, but explanations take time and the thing still needs doing. If they put it right, I'll notice. I don't want to promise in advance how quickly that will change my next request.

middle.text: I try to find out whether they understood what I was relying on. People can be surprisingly vague about a promise they remember making clearly. If we can agree on what happened, there's somewhere to start. I don't enjoy the part where I have to make the disappointment sufficiently convincing before it counts as an event.

high.text: I usually give them a chance to answer for it. Sometimes the answer is disappointing too. I can handle somebody saying they couldn't manage, even saying they didn't want to. I find it harder when they explain that I never really needed the thing. That makes it difficult to ask them anything honest afterward.

questions.label: What do you tend to keep to yourself?

low.text: Other people's things, if they've asked me to. My own things are less organised. An unfinished thought can escape into a conversation before I've decided whether I agree with it. I don't think every sentence needs to be ready for printing. That can be inconvenient when somebody decides to remember the one I would have corrected five minutes later.

middle.text: The amount of preparation. I might tell you what I want, but not how many times I have already explained it to an imaginary, more difficult version of you. I'd like the actual conversation to get a fair chance. It isn't your fault that I practised against somebody who kept interrupting.

high.text: Anything I want enough that a joke would stay with me. I can talk about a finished thing more easily. Wanting is awkward because there isn't evidence yet. People can supply a whole account of why you want it, and suddenly you're arguing about a person they invented instead of the small thing you were trying to do.

questions.label: What would you attempt without an audience?

low.text: Something I could abandon halfway without having to make the abandoning sound deliberate. Perhaps I'd learn how to repair a small object badly. I like the idea of an afternoon that leaves no announcement behind. If the object works at the end, lovely. If not, I'd like to be allowed to put it back in the drawer.

middle.text: A version with a bit more room in it. I'd keep the unnecessary part instead of cutting it before someone can ask what it's for. Then I'd see whether I still liked it a week later. I don't know that an audience always spoils things. I would just enjoy meeting the thing before it meets anybody else.

high.text: Probably the same difficult thing, with less time spent explaining why it's worth doing. I wouldn't become wonderfully relaxed just because nobody was watching. I'd still know where the bad part was. But I could stay with it longer, and the first version could be properly bad instead of already arranged to look promising.
